name: Roman travertine (Travertino Romano; the lapis Tiburtinus of Tivoli)
summary: A banded, porous limestone laid down as calcite by carbon-dioxide-rich thermal springs in the plain below Tivoli, east of Rome, and quarried there since antiquity. It is the museum's stone: sawn vein-cut, honed on walls and plinths, polished where a floor holds a reflection, and laid as the threshold of every doorway.

class.text: A chemical sedimentary rock: travertine is a precipitate of calcium carbonate from saturated, generally warm or hot, fresh, mineral-laden waters in and around the mouths of fractures; Tivoli's is an endogenic (thermogene) travertine.

formation.how: Thermal water rising along a fault from depth near the Colli Albani volcano carries calcium bicarbonate. At the surface it loses carbon dioxide and calcite precipitates in thin crusts, layer on layer, over vents, pools and terraces, trapping gas bubbles. The layers stack into depositional benches separated by erosional surfaces; the gaps between crusts and the gas bubbles become the stone's voids.

specularF0.conditions: normal incidence from air, 589.3 nm (0.0536 at 550 nm)
specularF0.derivation: F = ((n - 1) / (n + 1))^2. A face cut through randomly oriented calcite grains: half the light meets n_o (F = 0.0613); half meets n_e(theta), with 1/n_e(theta)^2 = cos^2(theta)/n_o^2 + sin^2(theta)/n_e^2, averaged over the sphere of grain orientations (mean F = 0.0453); 0.5 x 0.0613 + 0.5 x 0.0453 = 0.0533. min is F(n_e) and max is F(n_o), the extremes a single grain shows.

wet.text: A wet face darkens: water in the pores and on the surface lowers the index step at the grains, and the water film traps diffusely reflected light by total internal reflection, so more of it is absorbed.
wet.source: Lekner J., Dorf M.C. (1988) 'Why some things are darker when wet', Applied Optics 27(7):1278-1280, https://doi.org/10.1364/AO.27.001278

photograph: Vein-cut: parallel, wavy bands of ivory, cream and honey along the slab, with voids drawn out along the bands like small lenses.
Cross-cut: no bands, but soft clouds of tone with rounded, irregular voids scattered over the face, larger than in vein-cut slabs.
Open voids read as dark dots and dashes; filled voids as flush patches, grey where cement was used, glossier where resin was.
Honed: broad, soft reflections with no sharp image. Polished: sharp reflections, and the stone darker and warmer than when honed.
Adjacent slabs are different slices of one bed: the tone and band character carry across a joint, the lines do not.
On floors, the gloss is lost along walking lines and at doorways first; voids near the face open there.

The old build's 'about 4 % of the face', read from the procedural Travertine009 image (windows/SourceArt/PBR/CREDITS.md, 'Derived maps'). Not a measurement of real stone.
The old build's void depth, from the same procedural image. Not a measurement.

Seen only in a search-engine summary of trade pages (EN 1926), not read at its source.
Needed by the surface law's wetting and drying; no measurement of Tivoli travertine was read.
No quarry block or bench dimensions for Tivoli were found.

No pendulum or friction measurement of Roman travertine was read. A search summary cites mean values of 18 to 24 for polished limestones (Coskun, Sariisik and Sariisik 2016, Cogent Engineering 3:1217821), not read at the source.
The dense-stone row does not describe open-pore travertine; no measurement was found.
Only a white marble's scattering and absorption were found (Jensen et al. 2001).
